hero.title: Magic Tools
hero.blurb: Two things I kept doing by hand: working out whether my mana base actually delivers, and translating what I mean into Scryfall syntax. Both are here, both are open source.
hero.jump1Note: Hypergeometric, with the curve drawn out
hero.jump2Note: Type a sentence, get Scryfall syntax

odds.heading: Draw odds
odds.blurb: Hypergeometric: every draw shrinks the library, so the odds move with it. Set your deck up and read the whole distribution, not just one number.
odds.copiesHint: e.g. 24 lands, or 4 copies of one card
odds.distributionLabel: Distribution — chance of drawing exactly n
odds.sentence: Drawing {{draws}} cards from {{deck}}, you hit at least {{atLeast}} {{thing}} {{percent}} of the time.

mana.heading: Mana sources
mana.blurb: The other half of a mana base: not how many lands, but how many of them make the right colour. Pick a cost and the turn you want it, and this is what the deck needs to carry.
mana.pipsHint: Only pips of this colour — 1CC is two, generic doesn't count
mana.mulliganLabel: Ship a hand with none of this colour
mana.mulliganHint: One mulligan, and only on a blank — the policy people actually follow
mana.sentence: {{sources}} sources casts {{cost}} on turn {{turn}} {{percent}} of the time.
mana.impossible: No number of sources reaches that for {{cost}} on turn {{turn}} — you can't hold more pips than cards drawn.
mana.deltaWith: Willing to ship a colourless hand? {{sources}} would do.
mana.deltaWithout: Never mulliganing for colour? You'd want {{sources}}.
mana.curveLabel: What each source count buys you
mana.caveat: This counts colour and nothing else: it keeps a seven-lander happily and never asks whether the hand can function. Published tables land a little lower because they model hand quality too. Read it as “will my colours show up”, not “is this hand keepable”.

hands.heading: Opening hands
hands.blurb: Keeps are joint decisions: two lands and a two-drop, not each on its own. Multiplying separate odds overstates it, because both are competing for the same seven cards.
hands.rowsHint: Set “want” to 0 to ignore a row. Kinds must not overlap — a card counts once.
hands.correlation: Multiplying the odds separately would say {{product}} — too high, because they compete for the same slots.
hands.marginalsLabel: Each on its own, then together
hands.empty: Set at least one “want” above to see the odds.
hands.overcommitted: Those kinds add up to {{claimed}} cards in a {{deck}}-card deck. They have to be separate groups, so trim them.
hands.caveat: Categories are treated as disjoint: a card is a land or a two-drop, never both. If your two-drops include lands, count them once and pick the group that matters for the decision.

finding.heading: Finding a card
finding.blurb: The other axis: not how many you'll have drawn, but when it turns up. This is the singleton question — a tutor, a combo piece, a Commander one-of.
finding.copiesHint: 1 for a singleton or a tutor target
finding.sentence: {{percent}} of your opening hands from {{deck}} cards already contain it.
finding.tableLabel: Chance you've seen it by the start of each turn

dj.title: Crate
dj.deck: A desktop app for the Rekordbox library you already have: stack filters, find what's broken, see the shape of it, hand a playlist back. It isn't built yet — this page is a description, not a download.
dj.deckShort: A desktop app for the Rekordbox library you already have. It isn't built yet — a description, not a download.

problem.heading: The collection you can't see
problem.body: A few thousand tracks in Rekordbox, and you know maybe two hundred of them by feel. The rest you find by scrolling. The harmonic mixing you do in your head, or off the key tag two bars before you need it — fine, until the next record has to be right the first time. Rekordbox will sort any column you ask it to; it won't tell you the shape of what you own.
problem.bodyShort: A few thousand tracks in Rekordbox, and you know maybe two hundred by feel. The key you hold in your head, two bars before you need it. Rekordbox will sort any column you ask it to; it won't tell you the shape of what you own.

mechanism.heading: Rekordbox already knows
mechanism.body: Every one of those things is already in the collection file: the BPM, the key, the rating, the date you added it, the cue points, the colour tags, every playlist you've ever made. Rekordbox will sort one column at a time. What it won't do is let you ask it anything — six conditions at once, or what the whole pile looks like. So this doesn't analyse your audio and it doesn't guess at your taste. It reads a file you already have and answers the questions you were already asking.
mechanism.bodyShort: All of it is already in the collection file — BPM, key, rating, cue points, every playlist you've made. Rekordbox sorts one column at a time; it won't let you ask it six things at once. So this doesn't analyse audio or guess at your taste. It reads a file you already have.

read.title: Reads your export. Writes nothing back.
read.body: You point it at the XML export Rekordbox already makes. It reads everything in there — every field, every playlist, every cue — and it opens the file for reading only. Re-export later and it shows you what was added, changed or removed since last time. Rekordbox stays the thing that's true.
read.caveat: The honest wart: Rekordbox doesn't document its own database, which is why this reads the export and not the real thing — and the export is the one you have to remember to make. A format that can change without notice is the part most likely to break, and the part I'd keep having to fix.

filters.title: Filters that stack
filters.body: Rekordbox sorts one column. This intersects as many as you like: 122–126 BPM, in 8A, four stars and up, house, added this year, never played, has cue points. Save the combination and it keeps filling itself as the collection grows. That last one — never played — is how you find the records you bought and forgot.

harmonic.title: Camelot, and what pitch buys you
harmonic.body: Pick a track and the wheel lights the moves: the two adjacent numbers and the relative mode. Push the pitch and it lights more — what becomes compatible at ±3%, and again at ±6%. Camelot, Open Key or musical notation, whichever you read.

health.title: The unglamorous list
health.body: Duplicates across different files. Paths that point at nothing. Tracks with no BPM, no key, no genre, no artwork. Files that were never analysed. Genre tags spelled four ways. Bitrates you'd rather not hear on a big system. Tracks with no cue points, and tracks in no playlist at all. Ordered by how much each one costs you in a booth, not by how many there are.

overview.title: The shape of what you own
overview.body: The BPM spread as a histogram, so the pile at 122 and the hole at 128 are things you see rather than suspect. Genres by count — usually where you find out that what you play and what you own parted company a while ago. Keys, labels, decades, how the collection grew, what you actually rate. The answer to "what have I got".

handoff.title: Then it hands it back
handoff.body: Build a shortlist out of any filter and export it as a Rekordbox playlist, so it lands back in Rekordbox, on the USB, in the booth. That's where this stops. It hands you the pool; the set is yours. Nothing here decides what comes next, and nothing here is going to.

status.heading: Where it actually is
status.body: Right now it's a name and a list of what it would do. No repository, nothing to download, and no date I'd trust enough to give you. It'll be a desktop application rather than a web page, because the collection file lives on your machine and I'd rather it stayed there. When there's something to open, it will be at this address.
status.bodyShort: Right now it's a name and a list of what it would do. No repository, nothing to download, no date I'd trust enough to give you. It'll be a desktop app: the collection file lives on your machine and I'd rather it stayed there.

legal.title: Cookies & privacy
legal.intro: The short version: this site sets no cookies, runs no analytics, and sends nothing about you to anyone. There is no banner to dismiss because there is nothing to consent to.

sections.heading: Cookies
body: None. This site does not set cookies — not for analytics, not for advertising, not for anything else.

sections.heading: What is stored on your device
body: Two things, and only if you ask for them. When you use the light/dark switch in the header, your choice is saved in your browser's local storage under the key walter-theme. When you change the language, that choice is saved under walter-lang. If you never touch either control, nothing is written at all.

Those values never leave your browser. Each holds a single word — light or dark, en or it. You can delete them at any time by clearing site data for this domain, and the site will simply follow your operating system's appearance setting and your browser's language again.

Under the ePrivacy Directive (Article 5(3)) storage like this does not require consent: it is set only in response to something you explicitly did, it holds a display preference rather than anything identifying, and it is not used to track you. That is why there is no cookie banner.

sections.heading: Third parties
body: None are contacted when the page loads. Fonts are served from this domain rather than a font CDN, precisely so that reading the page does not disclose your IP address to anyone else. There are no embedded videos, maps, comment widgets, social scripts, or tracking pixels.

The page does contain ordinary links to GitHub, Twitch, Instagram, LinkedIn, Bandcamp and Spotify. Nothing is sent to those services unless you click a link and go there yourself, at which point their own policies apply.

sections.heading: The Magic Tools search
body: The plain-English search on the Magic Tools page sends the sentence you type — and nothing else — to a translation service run for this site, which turns it into Scryfall syntax. It is sent only when you press Translate, never as you type. The sentence is not stored against you or used to build a profile.
Following the resulting link takes you to scryfall.com, which is a separate service with its own privacy policy.

sections.heading: The "propose a tool" form
body: That form has no backend. Nothing you type is transmitted anywhere or stored on any server — when you submit it, your browser opens a draft in your own email client with the details filled in. Nothing is sent until you press send yourself, and if you close the draft, that is the end of it.

sections.heading: Server logs
body: This site is served by Firebase Hosting, a Google service, which keeps standard web-server logs of requests — IP address, timestamp, requested file, user agent. These are generated by the act of serving a page to you, are used only to deliver the site and keep it working, and are not combined with anything else or used to build a profile.

sections.heading: Your rights
body: Since no personal data is collected or stored here beyond the server logs described above, there is generally nothing to access, correct or delete. If you would like to ask about those logs, or anything else on this page, email lordLiniDev@proton.me.

seasonable.title: Seasonable
seasonable.deck: Tell it where you are and what month it is, and it names the fruit and vegetables genuinely in season there. It isn't built yet — this page is a description, not a link.
seasonable.deckShort: A place and a month in; what's genuinely in season there out. Not built yet — a description, not a link.

s1.heading: The strawberries in January
s1.body: You buy the thing because it's there. Strawberries in January, tomatoes in March — they look right under the shop lights, and then they taste of almost nothing and you cook them into something else to hide it. Working out what's actually in season is not hard, exactly. It's just that the answer changes with the month and with where you're standing, and the chart pinned in your head is the one from wherever you grew up.
s1.bodyShort: You buy the thing because it's there. Strawberries in January, tomatoes in March: right under the shop lights, then a taste of almost nothing. The answer changes with the month and with where you're standing, and the chart in your head is the one from wherever you grew up.

s2.heading: What it would do
s2.body: Two fields — a place and a month — and a short list back: what is being picked near you now, what is stored from earlier in the year, and what is only on the shelf because it flew. Nothing to log into, nothing to install.
s2.bodyShort: Two fields, a place and a month, and a short list back: what's being picked near you now, what's stored from earlier, and what's only there because it flew.
s2.caveat: The hard part is the word genuinely. A calendar for Italy is wrong for Sicily and for Piedmont at the same time, greenhouse and open field are different answers to the same question, and a warm year moves everything by two weeks. An honest version has to say where each date came from and how narrow the claim is. That is most of the work, and most of why it isn't written yet.
s2.caveatShort: The hard part is the word genuinely. A calendar for Italy is wrong for Sicily and for Piedmont at once, and a warm year moves everything by two weeks. Saying where each date came from is most of the work — and most of why it isn't written yet.

s3.heading: Where it actually is
s3.body: Right now it's a name and a page of notes. No repository, nothing to open, and no date I'd trust enough to give you. It would be a small web page, free, with the source there to read — the same as everything else here. When there is something to use, it will be at this address.
s3.bodyShort: Right now it's a name and a page of notes. No repository, nothing to open, no date I'd trust enough to give you. It would be a small free web page with readable source, like everything else here. When there's something to use, it will be here.
